summary: This RFC defines an XML-based data model for conference objects in centralized conferencing (XCON), which RFC 5239 describes as participants associated with a central focus. The model carries information about a conference and about who takes part in it. Other XCON protocols build on it.

plainLanguage.summary: A conference call needs a list of what the meeting is and who is in it. This is a standard form for that list, so different programs can fill it in and read it the same way.

questions: what is the xcon conference object
what is the conference information data model
subtitle: The XML document format that describes a centralized conference: its schedule, media, floors and participants.

tldr.problem: Centralized conferencing needs one common description of a conference, independent of media. The earlier SIP conference-state format is SIP specific and has no floor control or scheduling elements.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6501 defines a conference object as an XML document, a superset of the RFC 4575 format. A RELAX NG schema is normative, and new elements live in the urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xcon-conference-info namespace.
tldr.outcome: Conferencing protocols can read and change the same conference object, identified by an xcon URI. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 6501 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2012. It has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: Why a Conference Data Model
sections.content:
Every conference has a core set of information that does not depend on the media used. RFC 6501 defines this conference information data model in XML. The conference object, a concept from the centralized conferencing framework (RFC 5239), is one instance of this model.

The SIP event package for conference state (RFC 4575) already has a data format, but it is SIP specific and lacks elements for things such as floor control. The new model is a superset of that format, so it supports other call signaling protocols besides SIP and covers all the functionality of the framework. It adds scheduling, media control and floor control elements, non-SIP URIs and localization of text elements.
sections.plainLanguage: An older form for describing a call only worked for one kind of phone system. This new form works for many kinds and has extra boxes, like who gets to speak.

sections.title: Format, Namespace and Identifiers
sections.content:
A conference object document MUST be XML 1.0 and MUST be encoded in UTF-8. The normative syntax is the RELAX NG schema in Section 5, and compliant messages MUST meet it. New elements use the namespace urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:xcon-conference-info.

The conference object identifier (XCON-URI) is the key to a specific conference object. Its syntax is "xcon" ":" [conf-object-id "@"] host. It acts as the top-level identifier that other protocol identifiers hang under, such as SIP, H.323 and tel URIs, or the BFCP conference ID. The BFCP conference ID has a 1:1 mapping to the XCON-URI, while the others may occur multiple times. A system may structure these relationships as it likes.

An XCON-URI is not designed to be resolved, and an application MUST NOT do a DNS lookup on its host part. For comparison, all components MUST be converted to lowercase and then compared character by character as in RFC 3986.
sections.plainLanguage: Each conference gets a name tag, like a locker number. Other tags, such as phone numbers, all point back to that one locker number. You cannot look the tag up on the internet; it is just a name.

sections.title: Structure of a Conference Object
sections.content:
Everything sits under a root <conference-info> element. Its children are <conference-description> (the conference as a whole), <host-info>, <conference-state>, <floor-information>, <users> and the sidebar elements <sidebars-by-ref> and <sidebars-by-val>. Many elements come unchanged from RFC 4575. The new ones are the focus of this RFC, and the 'state' and 'version' attributes from RFC 4575 are not used because they apply only to notification mechanisms.

In <conference-description>, the new elements include <language>, <allow-sidebars>, <cloning-parent>, <sidebar-parent> and <conference-time>. Each <conference-time> entry holds an iCalendar object in <base> (RFC 5545) plus mixing start and end offsets, join-window offsets and an end-of-conference warning in seconds. Unlike plain iCalendar, it can set different join policies for the same conference at different times.

<conf-uris> entries gain a <conference-password>, such as a PSTN PIN code. <available-media> entries gain <mixing-mode> (moderator-controlled, FCFS or automatic), <codecs> and <controls>. The basic controls are <mute>, <pause-video>, <gain> (an integer from -127 to 127) and <video-layout>, whose default SHOULD be single-view.
sections.plainLanguage: The conference form has one big folder with smaller folders inside: one about the meeting, one about the host, one about who may speak, and one for each person.

sections.title: Floors, Users and Admission Policy
sections.content:
If <floor-information> is absent, the conference has no floor. Otherwise it carries the <conference-ID> (a 32-bit BFCP conference identifier when BFCP is used), <allow-floor-events> (default false), <floor-request-handling> (block by default, or confirm) and a <conference-floor-policy>. Each <floor> has a mandatory <media-label> and <algorithm> (moderator-controlled, FCFS or random), and optionally <max-floor-users> and <moderator-id>.

In <users>, <join-handling> tells the focus what to do with a join request: block (the default), confirm, allow, authenticate or directed-operator. <user-admission-policy> is one of three values:

  • closedAuthenticated: only authenticated users on the allowed users list may join, and any deny list is ignored.
  • openAuthenticated: any authenticated user may join, a deny list can ban users, and any allowed list is ignored.
  • anonymous: any join request is granted, and both lists are ignored.

The <allowed-users-list> holds <target> entries with a uri and a method of dial-in, dial-out or refer. Each <user> is identified by an XCON-USERID of the form "xcon-userid" ":" conf-user-id. It can have a <provide-anonymity> level (private, semi-private or hidden), roles, and permissions to refer, invite or remove users dynamically, all false by default.
sections.plainLanguage: The form also says who gets to talk and who may come in. A club might be open to anyone, only to members, or only to people on a guest list, and some people can ban troublemakers.

sections.title: Schema and Extensibility
sections.content:
The normative RELAX NG schema is in Section 5 of the RFC, and valid RFC 5239 instance documents are also valid under it. A non-normative RELAX NG schema in XML syntax and a W3C XML Schema are given in appendices.

The model is meant to be extended. Extensions are elements or attributes from namespaces other than the two conference-info namespaces, placed wherever the schema allows anyAttribute or anyElement. Elements or attributes from unknown namespaces MUST be ignored. Section 7 of the RFC then gives a full example document for a weekly Formula-1 discussion with three participants, one sidebar and one floor.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone wants to add a new box to the form, they can, as long as they put it under their own label. Programs that do not know the label just skip it.

sections.title: Security and Registrations
sections.content:
The authentication and identity privacy considerations of RFC 5239 apply, as do the authorization considerations of the SIP REFER method (RFC 3515). Each protocol used with a conference object may have its own authentication, so the conferencing system must map them to the same user. The mapping database to XCON-USERIDs must be protected: only authorized users may connect, and its integrity MUST be protected. The XCON-USERID or XCON-URI SHOULD be hard to guess.

Long-term storage SHOULD be encrypted, sensitive elements such as passwords MUST be kept confidential, and access over encrypted channels such as TLS is RECOMMENDED. Administrators should also avoid disclosing information when a conference is cloned or a sidebar is created. The privacy policy itself is left to future documents.

IANA registrations cover the RELAX NG schema, the XML namespace, and two URI schemes: xcon and XCON-USERID.
sections.plainLanguage: The guest list and the secret codes must be kept safe. Meeting names should be hard to guess, so strangers cannot just wander into someone else's call.

viz.caption: TOP-LEVEL STRUCTURE OF A CONFERENCE OBJECT

items.label: Closed
items.desc: Each participant must be on the allowed users list and authenticated; a deny list is ignored.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Any authenticated user may join; a deny list can ban users and an allowed list is ignored.

items.label: Anonymous
items.desc: Grants any join request; both lists are ignored.
